case_name: Levitts Kosher Foods Inc. v. Levin
text:
Levitts Kosher Foods Inc. v. Levin et al.

[Indexed as: Levitts Kosher Foods Inc. v. Levin]

45 O.R. (3d) 147

[1999] O.J. No. 2785

Court File No. 99-CV-163952-CM

Ontario Superior Court of Justice

Benotto J.

July 27, 1999

Civil procedure -- Stay of proceedings -- Plaintiff's claim not justiciable by court -- Defendants members of religious organization -- Defendants certifying whether foods complying with its interpretation of Jewish religious laws about diet and preparation of food -- Plaintiff selling kosher food products -- Defendants not certifying plaintiff's food products as meeting its standards -- Plaintiff alleging that defendants' actions libellous and in restraint of trade -- Plaintiff's claim in its essence involving matters of religious belief and conscience -- Plaintiff's claims not justiciable by the courts -- Court exercising discretion to stay action.
The defendants were three Toronto rabbis who were part of the Vaad Hakashruth, a Toronto council of orthodox rabbis, which sets standards for the preparation of food in accordance with its interpretation of kashrut, a detailed and complex body of Jewish religious law about diet and the preparation of food consistent with Jewish religious observance, spirituality, and the quest for a holy life. The Vaad Hakashruth, like similar supervisory rabbinical organizations in other communities throughout the world, granted certifications that a food complied with its standards. A Vaad Hakashruth certification was indicated to consumers by the use of the symbol "COR". The Vaad Hakashruth had adopted a policy of shomer Shabbat, which was a policy that, subject to certain exceptions for previously certified establishments, a food vendor, or, if a corporation, its human principal, be a person who is strictly observant of the tenets and requirements of Jewish law , and a policy of shechitas chutz, which was a policy that meat imported from other communities would not be certified and only slaughterers, butchers, and food establishments within the local community would be certified. Observant Jews relied on Vaad Hakashruth certification, but the absence of certification did not mean that a food was not kashrut, and a consumer might rely on a certification from another supervising body that would use its own distinctive symbol.
The plaintiff LKF Inc. was a Montreal company that produced and sold kosher meat and deli products. Its products had been certified by other supervising councils, including the Va'ad Ha Ir of Montreal, as having the highest standards of kashrut. Under an exception to the shomer Shabbat policy, its deli meats were sold in Toronto in COR establishments.
In early 1997, the Vaad Hakashruth took steps to enforce its shechitas chutz policy. This had the effect of preventing COR establishments from selling LKF Inc.'s fresh meat, and LKF Inc., without formally requesting certification, sought to have the exception, which had been made available for its deli products, applied to its fresh meat. When this was refused, LKF Inc. sued the defendants, who formed the Vaad Hakashruth. LKF Inc. alleged that the shechitas chutz policy violated restraint of trade laws and that the defendants' communications to COR establishments were libellous. The defendants moved for a stay of the action on the ground that the questions to be decided were intrinsically religious and not justiciable.
Held, the motion for a stay should be granted.
Courts are reluctant to intervene in the internal matters of a religious body and to deprive it of the right to interpret its own doctrine. While, on the surface, LKF Inc.'s claim appeared to fall within the ambit of property and civil rights, the essence of the claim was an attack on the shomer Shabbat and the shechitas chutz policies of the Vaad Hakashruth. To assert its claims, LKF Inc. raised the profoundly religious issues of the authority of the rabbis, their interpretation of the laws of kashrut, their views of the trustworthiness of non-observant Jews, and the standards which they, as a matter of conscience, believed necessary to fulfill their obligations. LKF Inc.'s claims showed a fundamental misunderstanding of the supervisory system. The Vaad Hakashruth did not determine if meat was kosher; rather, it determined whether meat satisfied its standards, which were set as a matter of the religious interpretation and conscience of the rabbis. LKF Inc.' s products were kosher, but they did not meet the standards of Vaad Hakashruth. The process of supervision and certification was a religious function, based on both objective and subjective criteria. It was a process based on trust, which was of particular importance given that the spiritual life of the community was at stake. The questions here were matters of religious belief and conscience. The continuance of the action would work an injustice to the defendants because LKF Inc.'s claims were not justiciable. Further, a stay would not cause an injustice to LKF Inc., which, operating in a religious environment, was subject to the religious laws that govern that environment. Having decided to operate its business within the orthodox community and, for many years, having taken the benefit of the system, it could not claim it was prejudiced by having to follow the rules of that system. It was not appropriate for the court to be involved in this dispute. The defendants had satisfied the court that the continuance of the action was oppressive, vexatious or an abuse of process and that a stay would not cause an injustice to the plaintiff. The motion for a stay should be granted.
MOTION for a stay of an action.

Cases referred to
Ben David v. Congregation B'Nai Israel, Ont. Gen. Div., Sharpe J., September 24, 1997 (unreported); Brewer v. Anglican Church of Canada Diocese of Ottawa,

Live Poultry Corp. v. Kashruth Assn. of Greater N.Y. Inc., 158 Misc. 358, 285 N.Y.S. 879; Uditsky v. Ottawa Vaad Hakashres
(1926), 31 O.W.N. 189 (C.A.)

211 N.E.2d 332 (Mass. 1965)

David Hager and Kenneth A. Krupat, for plaintiff.
Joel Richler and Jeffrey Galway, for defendants.

BENOTTO J.: -- Levitts Kosher Foods Inc. is a Montreal
company which produces and sells kosher meat. It has sued
three Toronto rabbis who are part of the council responsible
for supervising and certifying products and establishments in
Toronto which, in its view, comply with Jewish dietary laws.
The plaintiff says, among other things, that the defendants'
policies contravene restraint of trade laws. The defendants
say that their policies are an intrinsic part of their
religious mandate to supervise the production and distribution
of food. Therefore, they say, the courts should not intervene
in the dispute. They bring this motion requesting that the
action be stayed.

The System of Supervision

Jewish dietary laws are known as the laws of kashrut. They
form one of the pillars of Jewish religious practice. They are
based on the first five books of the Bible, the Talmud, and
various codes of Jewish law and rulings made by rabbinical
scholars for many centuries. The laws are complex and
detailed. They reflect the belief that food has a direct
effect on character, moral disposition and holiness. To an
observant Jew, even an unintentional transgression of dietary
laws can undermine religious observance, spirituality and the
quest for a holy life.

Observant Jews rely on rabbinical organizations to supervise
and certify the kashrut of their food. The supervisory body's
role is to ensure that the producer uses permitted
ingredients, permitted modes of preparation and proper
equipment. Such organizations exist in various communities
throughout the world. Each supervising body has its own
distinctive mark or logo so that the consumer can tell if the
product is supervised by a trusted organization.

The Vaad Hakashruth is the Toronto council of 11 orthodox
rabbis, which determines whether, according to its policies,
products and establishments comply with the laws of kashrut.
It, like other supervising agencies, has particular standards.
Producers and establishments who wish to be certified must
meet the standards set by the supervising body. Certification
by the Vaad Hakashruth is signaled to the consumer by the
symbol "COR" which is affixed to products. Businesses which
are certified can advertise themselves and their products as
being under "COR" supervision and are only allowed to sell or
use products, ingredients or methods of preparation which are
themselves COR certified or otherwise acceptable to the Vaad
Hakashruth.

Other supervisory bodies, in other communities use their own
symbols to verify certification, for example: OU (Orthodox
Union), Star-K (Star-K Kosher Certification -- Baltimore) and
MK (Montreal Kosher). The standards of these organizations may
vary. Some are stricter than others are. There is no
obligation on a supervisory body to accept the certification
of another.

Compliance with COR supervision is only necessary for those
establishments and businesses which apply for and are granted
COR certification. There are other food establishments and
products in Toronto which are held out as kosher on the
strength of a kashrut endorsement by another supervising body.
There are observant consumers who rely on those other
endorsements, presumably because they are satisfied with the
standards applied by those supervising bodies.

The Vaad Hakashruth will only certify another supervisory
body's products where the supervisory body known to the Vaad,
is highly trustworthy and applies the same standards of
kashrut.

In recent years, there has been a return to meticulousness
in the observance of the precepts of Judaism. The more
knowledgeable and pious consumers raised their expectations of
the Vaad Hakashruth. They wished more stringent levels of
observance. In response to these demands, the Vaad Hakashruth
and the Kashruth Council adopted policies, two of which are
relevant to these proceedings. They are the shomer Shabbat
policy and the shechitas chutz policy.

Shomer Shabbat

Shomer Shabbat means "observant of the Sabbath". It is used
to describe a person who is strictly observant of the tenets
and requirements of Jewish law. The Vaad Hakashruth believes
that a person who is not shomer Shabbat does not have the same
credibility as someone who is.

Central to the certification process is the element of
trust. The rabbi or supervisory agency has to have trust in
the person or company seeking certification. The observant
community has to have trust that the certifying agency applies
standards which are acceptable. Supervisory bodies know that
it is virtually impossible to provide constant supervision.
Thus they are given broad powers and discretion to assess the
trustworthiness of the proprietors of a business seeking
certification. According to Rabbi Bleich, a highly respected
scholar, professor, author and expert on Jewish law, neither
the rabbi nor the supervisory body can grant certification,
even to an ostensibly qualified applicant, where the requisite
degree of trust has not been established. A rabbi or
supervisory body is entitled to demand those stringencies that
he or it thinks appropriate on behalf of the community.

The Vaad Hakashruth sought greater assurance that the laws
of kashrut would be observed. In its view, someone who is
shomer Shabbat would offer that assurance, as the possibility
of both advertent and inadvertent errors would be diminished.
In short, the person and business would be more trustworthy.
So it was that in about 1985, the Vaad Hakashruth adopted the
requirement that any applicant for certification be shomer
Shabbat. In the case of corporations, the controlling
shareholders must be shomer Shabbat. Under Jewish law, the
personal religious observance of the proprietor of a business
cannot be divorced from the issue of whether that business
will fully adhere to the laws of kashrut.

There are several supervisory bodies in other cities which
have adopted this policy including the Bet Din of London,
England; the Kashruth Division of Orthodox Union, in the
United States (one of the biggest supervisory bodies in the
world) and the Va'ad Ha Ir in Montreal.

In order to avoid hardship to previously certified
establishments which were not shomer Shabbat, but which had
demonstrated adherence to the laws, the Vaad Hakashruth made
exceptions to the policy. It used its discretion to
"grandfather" those that had established a long and
trustworthy relationship. For those establishments, their
pre-existing COR certification was not revoked. Other
supervisory bodies which adopted the shomer Shabbat policy
also used the grandfather exception.

Shechitas Chutz

In implementing the laws of kashrut, it is important for
each community to have a dependable supply of kosher meat.
Historically this was accomplished, in part, by restricting
the importation of fresh meat to the community. When
slaughterers operate in distant cities and towns, kashrut
supervision is more difficult and costly to arrange and
maintain. Given the variations in standards among different
supervisory bodies, many supervisory bodies insist on personal
supervision to ensure that their standards of kashrut are
followed.

Thus, it is not uncommon for supervising rabbis to follow a
shechitas chutz policy. Literally translated, it means
"outside slaughtering". Figuratively, the expression refers to
the practice of certifying only slaughterers within the
community and not certifying those from outside. Rabbi Bleich
stated that the policy is concerned with the laws of kashrut
and also with ensuring a reliable source of supply for a
community. He stated that supervisory bodies have historically
given preference to slaughterers, butchers and food
establishments within their communities. These policies were
based upon the degree of confidence that can only come from
personal knowledge and verification and the need to assure a
reliable local supply of acceptable food products on a
continuous basis. He explained that rabbinical authorities
have very broad authority to impose whatever measures they
deem necessary in order to assure compliance with the
regulations of Jewish law and in order to assure observance of
the laws of kashrut.

The defendant Rabbi Kerzner said that in adopting the
shechitas chutz policy, the Vaad Hakashruth wanted to maintain
a local supply of kosher meat and control over the standards
of meat production. The rabbis were concerned that meat
imported from other sources would not be subject to the same
standards being imposed locally. Ever present was the concern
about differing standards.

As is the case with the shomer Shabbat policy, the shechitas
chutz policy is followed by other rabbis and supervisory
bodies around the world including the Va'ad Ha Ir of Montreal
and the Bet Din of London, England. In fact, in contrast to
the policy adopted by the Va'ad Ha Ir of Montreal, which
allows no imported fresh meat to be sold in the City of
Montreal, the Vaad Hakashruth has adopted a more flexible
shechitas chutz policy. In cases where there is a need for
additional sources of fresh meat, the Vaad Hakashruth has
allowed the importation of fresh meat from other
jurisdictions.

The Plaintiff's Business

The plaintiff corporation was originally operated by the
Levitts family in Montreal. By the end of 1983, the Levitts no
longer owned shares of the business and Mr. Brookman and Mr.
Herscovici became equal shareholders. By 1991, Mr. Katz had
purchased the shares of Mr. Herscovici. Since then, Mr.
Brookman and Mr. Katz have been operating the company as equal
shareholders and are the current principals. They are not
shomer Shabbat.

The company produces and sells fresh kosher meat and meat
products such as "deli" meats. The production takes place in
Montreal. Its meat is sold throughout Canada and abroad. The
company also has its own store in the Toronto area on Alness
Drive between Finch and Steeles Avenues West.

The plaintiff's products have been certified by the Va'ad Ha
Ir of Montreal and bear its symbol "MK". They have also been
certified by the Orthodox Jewish Council Vaad Hakashrus and
bear its symbol "Star-K". These two supervising authorities
have certified the meat as glatt kosher which signifies the
highest standards of kashrut.

Since 1977, the plaintiff's deli-products have been for sale
in COR establishments in Toronto. Although the plaintiff's
principals were not shomer Shabbat, the sale of deli products
continued after 1985 under the grandfather policy. The deli
products, in the view of the defendants, do not require the
same high level of security as do fresh meats. They are,
however, subject to the requirement that each shipment must be
personally endorsed by Rabbi Jaffe, the COR assigned kashrut
supervisor in Montreal.

The plaintiff has never applied to the Vaad Hakashruth for
certification of its fresh (as distinct from deli) meats.
Instead, it sells fresh meat in non-COR supervised
establishments and through its Alness Drive store relying on
its MK and Star-K certification.

In early 1997, the Kashruth Council took steps to enforce
its shechitas chutz policy. This had the effect of preventing
establishments under its supervision from selling the
plaintiff's fresh meat. Memos were sent to COR establishments
indicating that non-compliance would risk revocation of COR
supervision. In February 1997, the Toronto Kashruth Council
advised establishments under its supervision that only glatt
kosher meat from Toronto approved sources could be sold in COR
establishments. The evidence of the plaintiff is that Mr. Katz
was told that Toronto was a "closed" city. This refers to the
shechitas chutz policy. It is common ground that Montreal is
also a closed city. (The plaintiff obtains the benefit of the
shechitas chutz policy there because businesses not in
Montreal are not certified.)

The plaintiff, while not formally requesting certification,
sought to obtain the benefit of the grandfather exception to
the shomer Shabbat policy for its fresh meat. However,
according to the defendants, the long and trustworthy
relationship had not been established. Firstly, the Vaad
Hakashruth never endorsed or knowingly allowed the sale of the
plaintiff's fresh meats in COR establishments. Secondly, the
current owners of the business, having operated the company
together since only 1991, do not have the history with the
Vaad that would justify the use of the grandfather exception.
The evidence is clear that in the case of a corporation, it is
the trustworthiness and character of the principals that the
Vaad Hakashruth will consider.

The plaintiff has sued three of the rabbis who form the Vaad
Hakashruth. It claims that the shechitas chutz policy violates
restraint of trade laws, and that the communications requiring
its establishments to stop selling its fresh meats were
libelous because they implied its food was not kosher. It
seeks an injunction and damages.

The defendants say that even if the shechitas chutz policy
were not in place, their decision with respect to
certification of the plaintiff's products would be the same
for it also violates the shomer Shabbat policy. It is
acknowledged that the owners of the plaintiff are not
observant Jews. The plaintiff says that their fresh meats
should be grandfathered just as their deli meats were.

The defendants take the position that the plaintiff's action
demonstrates a total lack of appreciation for the
certification process and its rationale. Worse still, the
institution of a lawsuit in the secular courts has violated
Jewish law and, according to the defendants, demonstrated
contempt for the precepts they seek to uphold.

These two positions have become further entrenched by the
events since the service of the claim. The rabbis, in
accordance with Jewish law, sought to have the jurisdictional
issue determined by a rabbinical court, the Bet Din. The
plaintiff was summoned to the court, ignored the summons and
was found in contempt. The plaintiff now points to this fact
as evidence of the potential prejudice it will suffer if its
only recourse is the Bet Din. The defendants view the actions
of the plaintiff in ignoring the summons and pursuing the
action in this court as a further proof that its owners do not
value the precepts of the Jewish faith. As a result, there has
been an even greater diminution in the requisite trust that
would be required for certification.

Analysis

The defendants ask the court to exercise its discretion to
stay the action. They say that the questions to be decided are
intrinsically religious and thus not justiciable and that the
plaintiff has impliedly consented to submit to the rabbinical
courts.

A stay of proceeding is granted rarely. In order to justify
a stay, the defendant must satisfy the court that continuance
of the action would work an injustice because it would be
oppressive or vexatious or an abuse of the process of the
court and that the stay would not cause an injustice to the
plaintiff.

Justiciability of the claim

The courts are understandably reluctant to intervene in the
internal matters of a religious body. To do so would deprive
the religious organization of the right to interpret its own
doctrine. [See Note 1 at end of document] Our courts have
consistently held that it is not appropriate for civil courts
to decide questions of religious doctrine. [See Note 2 at end
of document] The Supreme Court of Canada has held that the
courts are slow to exercise jurisdiction over religious
groups. [See Note 3 at end of document] In adjudicating Church
disputes, the court will not look to the merits of the
decision, but rather looks at adherence to the rules,
procedural fairness and the absence of mala fides and natural
justice. [See Note 4 at end of document] The courts will
intervene, however, where the matter is one of property or
civil rights and the dispute can be resolved according to
applicable civil law principles.

On the surface, the plaintiff's claim falls within the ambit
of property and civil rights. The civil causes of action
pleaded are libel and slander, breach of contract,
interference with economic relations, conspiracy and restraint
of trade. These allegations, however, do not disclose the real
issues to be determined. Those issues must be identified
before there can be a consideration of the appropriateness of
court involvement.

Although couched in property and civil rights terms, the
essence of the plaintiff's claim is an attack on the shomer
Shabbat and the shechitas chutz policies. All of the
plaintiff's claims flow from the implementation by the rabbis
of those policies. Those policies were set by the Vaad
Hakashruth as part of their mandate to supervise the kashrut
of food. To assert their claims, the plaintiff must call into
question the supervisory authority of the rabbis, their
interpretation of the laws of kashrut, their views as to the
trustworthiness of non-observant Jews, and the standards which
they, as a matter of conscience, believe are necessary to
fulfill their obligations. These issues are profoundly
religious.

In the exercise of their supervisory functions, the rabbis
may affect the property and civil rights of the plaintiff.
However, the plaintiff has chosen to operate its business in a
religious context. The food it produces has a deeply religious
significance to the Jewish Orthodox community. It is therefore
subject to severe restraints and the control of the religious
leaders. As stated by a New York court:

In the very nature of things, kashruth must be a monopoly in
the hands of those best qualified to administer it. By
definition and tradition those persons are the rabbis, and
their decree is final. [See Note 5 at end of document]

The plaintiff argues that the issue is the conduct of the
defendants, through restrictive trade practices, in preventing
the sale of fresh meat to businesses it supervises. This
discloses a fundamental misunderstanding of the supervisory
system. The Vaad Hakashruth does not determine if meat is
kosher. It determines whether meat satisfies its standards.
Those standards are set as a matter of religious
interpretation and conscience of the rabbis. The supervisory
function is part of the leadership authority given to the
rabbis by Jewish law and is expected of them by their
congregations. It is agreed that the plaintiff's products are
kosher, having been certified by other supervisory bodies.
They do not, however, meet the standards of Vaad Hakashruth.
There is no obligation on the Vaad to certify all kosher food.
On the contrary, there is an obligation on it to ensure that
all the food it certifies meets the standards that it
considers necessary.

The process of supervision and certification is a religious
function, based on objective and subjective criteria. It is a
process based on trust which is of particular importance given
that the spiritual life of the community is at stake.

The plaintiff relies primarily on the 1926 case of Uditsky
[See Note 6 at end of document] where the Court of Appeal of
Ontario held that the plaintiff's claim against the Kashruth
Council for conspiracy and slander should proceed to trial. In
that case, a rabbinical court held that the plaintiff had
violated Jewish law in the production of meat. He alleged that
he had refused to increase the price of meat as required by
the rabbis and as a result the defendants conspired to and did
slander him and cause injury to his business. The defendants
pleaded that all parties to the action were governed by Jewish
law, that everything done by the defendants were done in
accordance with Jewish law, that they acted in good faith
without malice and with the object of observing their
religion. They also set up a defence of privilege and
justification. The case went to trial in the civil courts. The
trial judge withdrew from the jury the consideration of
conspiracy. The Court of Appeal ordered a new trial on the
issue of conspiracy and slander. The issue appears to be
whether there was evidence for the trial judge to send parts
of the case to the jury. Thus, the case does not assist me in
determining how courts determine whether a matter is concerned
with religious doctrine to such an extent that the courts
should decline to be involved in the first place.

The plaintiff also referred to an endorsement of Sharpe J.
(as he then was) where he declined to grant a stay of the
action "solely on the basis that both parties adhere to the
same body of religious belief". [See Note 7 at end of
document] The case here goes far beyond those facts. Here at
issue is the rabbis' ability to make religious policies
flowing from and as part of their interpretation of religious
doctrine. The request for a stay is a result of the issue to
be determined, not the religion of the litigants.

The courts will inquire into decisions made by
ecclesiastical bodies to determine whether the decision is in
compliance with the laws and authority of the Church. Here,
however, the attack is not on the procedure but on the rules
themselves. The evidence is that the Vaad Hakashruth, and
other supervisory bodies, have the power to make the shomer
Shabbat and the shechitas chutz policies.

The establishment clause of the First Amendment of the
United States Constitution which provides that "Congress shall
make no law respecting the establishment of religion" has been
interpreted as prohibiting secular government authorities from
deciding theological disputes between competing views of
religious law. The state can neither impose religious rules
nor endorse religious norms and can not lend its power to one
side or the other in controversies over religious authority or
dogma. I view the American cases in this context. However, I
find the statements in the jurisprudence instructive.

In United Kosher Butchers Association v. Associated
Synagogues of Greater Boston, Inc., [See Note 8 at end of
document] an association of kosher retail meat stores sought
to enjoin the defendant, a kashrut supervisory body, from
advising stores under its supervision not to buy the meat
produced by the plaintiffs. In declining to intervene the
court said (at p. 334):

. . . this court is not qualified to decide and therefore
must refuse to consider an issue which is so exclusively one
of religious practice and conscience.

In Korn v. Rabbinical Council of California, [See Note 9 at
end of document] the rabbinical supervisory body was sued
when, having formed the opinion that the plaintiff's meat was
not kosher, the Rabbinical Council removed its certification
and placed an advertisement in a newspaper circulated in the
Jewish community announcing that the plaintiff's meat no
longer warranted the supervisory body's endorsement. In
upholding the lower court's decision to strike the complaint,
the appeal court said (at p. 914):

. . . as autonomous entities, defendants are entitled to
their own opinions and are obligated by the authority vested
in them by the community which they serve to make known
their opinion concerning whether the particular food
products conform with the Judaic dietary laws.

The plaintiff relies on the Cabinet v. Shapiro case. [See
Note 10 at end of document] There, the plaintiff sold kosher
poultry. The local supervisory body invoked a shechitas chutz
policy and required that all fowl be slaughtered locally. The
defendants made statements that the plaintiff's chickens were
not kosher. The Superior Court of New Jersey decided to hear
the claim for libel because the property and civil rights of
the plaintiffs were involved.

Both the issue and the evidence in that case appear to
differ from the case here. Firstly, here it is admitted that
the plaintiff's food is kosher. It simply does not meet the
standards of the defendants because of the shomer Shabbat and
shechitas chutz policies. Secondly the evidence here is that
different supervisory bodies have different standards and
there is no obligation to accept the certification of another
body. The evidence must have been different in the Cabinet
case for the court said, "if kosher in one place of the world
must be kosher in each hamlet and community." This does not
address the issue of the varying standards applied by
supervisory bodies.

The issue here is one of religious belief and conscience. I
conclude that the action is one where continuance would work
an injustice to the defendants because the claims are not
justiciable and are thus oppressive, vexatious, and an abuse
of process.

Prejudice to the plaintiff

The defendant must also establish that a stay would not
cause an injustice to the plaintiff. The plaintiff operates
within a religious environment. It is subject to the religious
laws which govern that environment. It receives benefits from
the laws by virtue of its MK and Star-K certification. It
receives an advantage over other businesses which do not have
that certification. The plaintiff now seeks to obtain the
advantages of the kosher business without assuming the
obligations which necessarily accompany such certification.
This goes squarely to the issue of prejudice. These principles
were articulated by the Supreme Judicial Court of
Massachusetts:

The plaintiff by . . . seeking to conduct a business with
respect to kosher food which plays a highly important part
in the faith of members of such congregations must conform
to the canons of that faith touching that subject if he
desires to continue that business under religious sanction.
He cannot hold or gain that kind of commercial advantage
unless he complies with all requirements of the rules
established by that religious sect as pre-requisite
therefor, and he must also abide by the decisions of the
tribunals erected and constituted for the determination of
controversies concerning that subject. He cannot claim the
benefits of the business without accepting the burdens
attached to it. As incidents of his membership in the
religious organization and his undertaking to do this
particular kind of business, he impliedly consented to be
governed in all essential matters by the decisions of boards
established to end disputes and contentions of this sort.11

The plaintiff argues that there can be no implied consent to
attend a rabbinical court because Bet Din proceedings are held
only when both parties have signed an agreement submitting to
the jurisdiction of the Bet Din. I agree that the plaintiff
cannot be forced to a Bet Din. However, the consent of the
plaintiff to abide by the authority of the rabbis is inherent
in its decision to operate a kosher food business and to seek
to sell its food in businesses which are supervised by them.

The plaintiff argues that a stay would prejudice them
because its only recourse would then be to attend the
rabbinical court where procedures are not the same as in the
civil court. However, this ignores the fact that Jewish law
requires that the rabbinical court determine such disputes.
Having decided to operate its business within the orthodox
community, and having for many years taken the benefit of the
system, it can not now claim it is prejudiced by following one
of its basic laws. Viewed in the religious context of the
business world that the plaintiff chose to operate in and
profit from, I cannot find that the plaintiff is prejudiced by
following the rules of that system.

The plaintiff's action is founded on the premise that the
religious policies of shomer Shabbat and shechitas chutz are
wrong. The defendants have implemented these policies in
fulfillment of their religious mandate. The policies only
apply to businesses and products that seek to be certified.
The plaintiff never sought certification. The plaintiff is,
indeed, free to continue to sell in non-COR establishments and
its own shop. If the plaintiff applies for certification,
implicit in the application would be the willingness to accept
the authority of the rabbis. It would be inappropriate for the
court in this case to interfere with the authority of the
rabbis.

In my view, it is not appropriate for the court to be
involved in this dispute. The claims of the plaintiff are not
justiciable, and a stay would not prejudice the plaintiff. I
grant the defendants' motion for a stay of proceedings.

If counsel cannot agree on costs, they may arrange, through
my secretary, to speak to me.

Order accordingly.
